headline: YouTube Shorts dropped minimum watch requirement for view counting in March 2025
stat: views count from first play, no minimum watch time
statContext: all Shorts views since March 2025, down from previous threshold
why: YouTube removed the watch-time floor that separated a counted view from a skip. This aligns Shorts counting with TikTok and Instagram, where a view fires immediately. The change makes vanity metrics rise but does not affect ranking—YouTube still weights satisfaction surveys and retention for recommendations. The timing matters because it preceded the August 24 threshold drop across all formats and the October 1 originality update, suggesting YouTube was systematically simplifying its counting rules before tightening quality filters.
move: Stop using raw view counts as a success signal for Shorts. Track click-through from impressions and average watch percentage instead, since those still predict whether YouTube promotes the video.

headline: YouTube began ranking original Shorts higher and suppressing re-uploads on October 1
stat: original content prioritised, re-uploads without added value get less reach
statContext: YouTube Shorts feed recommendations starting October 1, 2026
why: YouTube updated its recommendation systems to 'further prioritize original content and reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own'. The mechanism is a new originality classifier in the ranker, not just duplicate detection—YouTube is judging whether you added creative value. This follows the March view-counting change and suggests YouTube is fighting the TikTok repost farms that flooded Shorts after monetisation opened. The move was predictable (every platform eventually does this) but the timing—right before the February 2027 revenue…
move: If you remix or compile others' clips, add substantive commentary, new editing or a unique angle. If you cannot add value, do not post it. Check your Shorts feed impressions in Analytics after October 1—a drop with stable CTR and retention means you were flagged.

headline: X's video-open weight rose from 0.05 to 0.07 while video quality view dropped to zero
stat: video_open weight 0.05 to 0.07, vqv weight 0.05 to 0.0
statContext: X's Phoenix ranking model default weights, commit on August 25, 2026
why: X simultaneously raised the credit for opening a video player and eliminated the bonus for watching to a quality threshold. The mechanism: X is rewarding the click more than the finish, which inverts typical short-form logic. This pairs with the binary dwell change (also August 25)—X now pays for initial interest (the open) and sustained attention (10-second dwell), but not for passive completion. The likely reason: completion is too easy to game with ultra-short clips, while open+dwell together signal real intent. The move contradicts creator advice to 'just make them watch to the end'.
move: For video on X: optimise your thumbnail and first frame to drive the open, then script the first ten seconds to hold attention through the dwell threshold. Stop worrying about finishing the clip—there is no ranking credit for it anymore.

headline: X accounts posting over 10 times daily see roughly 14% lower engagement per post
stat: 14% lower engagement per post above 10 posts/day
statContext: brand accounts in one third-party posting-frequency analysis, date not specified
why: This is audience fatigue, not an algorithmic penalty. The same follower base cannot engage with every post when volume is high, so each additional post past the ceiling returns less. The mechanism: your followers' feeds fill with your content, they skip more of it, and the ranker sees lower predicted engagement on each piece. The finding contradicts 'post as much as possible' advice but aligns with X's reply/retweet-heavy ranking—conversations need time to develop. The source is thin (one unnamed analysis, no date, no methodology), so treat this as a rough benchmark, not a law.
move: If you post more than 10 times a day, audit whether each post is genuinely earning replies and shares. If engagement per post is dropping, cut frequency and raise quality—fewer posts that spark conversation will outrank more posts that get passive likes.

headline: X's ranker now rewards ten-second click-dwell instead of passive impressions
stat: click-dwell weight set to 1.0 in default config, binary trigger at 10 seconds
statContext: X's Phoenix ranker configuration as of September 2026, affects how clicks on posts are scored
why: X added a click-dwell head that only fires positive if the viewer stays at least ten seconds after clicking. This replaces the old model where any click counted equally. The mechanism: a viewer who clicks a link and bounces after four seconds fires nothing; one who stays eleven seconds fires the head. This aligns with the August 25 binary dwell change—X is systematically rewarding attention duration over passive actions. The platform wants engagement that holds people on-platform or demonstrates genuine interest, not reflexive taps.
move: If you share links, write captions that make people want to stay and discuss rather than immediately clicking through. Test posting the link in a reply instead of the main post so the click-through doesn't kill the parent post's distribution.

headline: X's Phoenix aggregation switched from short dwell to long dwell as the default
stat: aggregation default changed from short dwell to long dwell
statContext: X's Phoenix ranking system configuration change, affects how dwell time signals are processed
why: The Phoenix aggregation setting controls how dwell signals are rolled up across a user's session. Switching the default from short to long dwell means the ranker now prioritizes sustained attention over quick glances. This is the third dwell-related change in the same update (binary dwell turned on, dwell weight raised to 0.05, and now this aggregation switch). The pattern is clear: X is systematically retuning every part of the ranking system that touches attention duration. Long dwell likely means they're measuring across a longer time window or weighting later seconds more heavily than the…
move: Optimize the first thirty seconds to hold attention, not just the first three. If you make threads, make the second and third posts worth reading—X may now be crediting you for keeping someone in the thread longer.

headline: X weights scale predicted probabilities not raw counts, one report does not cancel hundreds of likes
stat: weights multiply the viewer's own predicted probability of each action
statContext: Explanation of how X's ranking weights work in the open-source code, clarifies common misconception
why: The ranking weights people see in X's code—like report at -1.5 and like at 0.5—do not mean one report literally cancels three likes. They scale the predicted probability that this specific viewer will take that action, which is calculated from the viewer's own past behavior. A viewer who never reports anything has a near-zero report probability, so even a high negative weight barely moves their score. This matters because it means controversial posts that get both loves and hates are not simply averaged—the system predicts whether you personally will like or report it based on your history…
move: Stop worrying about getting reported by people who were never going to engage positively. Focus on creating content that your actual audience—the people whose behavior predicts they will engage—wants to see. Polarization is not inherently penalized if the right half loves it.

headline: TikTok judges each video independently; same account's best and worst posts differ massively in reach
stat: 58 creators' best vs worst recent posts showed wide variance within same account
statContext: September 2026 sample via TokConnect of ten recent posts each across six niches
why: If TikTok's algorithm penalized or boosted at the account level, one creator's videos would cluster around a similar view count. They do not. The same account can have one video hit 500K and the next hit 8K. This confirms what TikTok has said but creators often doubt: the algorithm does not remember your last video's performance when ranking the new one. Each video enters the same cold-start test regardless of whether your previous post flopped or went viral. The mechanism is economic—TikTok wants to fill the For You feed with the best content right now, and past performance is a weak…
move: Do not let a low-performing video discourage you from posting the next one. Each video gets a fair shot. Test more concepts rather than trying to reverse-engineer why the last one failed—the algorithm does not care about your last one.

headline: X raised video-open weight and turned on binary dwell while killing quality-view finish bonus
stat: video_open weight went 0.05 to 0.07, dwell went 0.0 to 0.05, vqv went 0.05 to 0.0
statContext: Three of twenty-six ranking weights in X's open-source algorithm, changed August 25, 2026
why: X stopped rewarding finish rates and started rewarding the open itself plus binary dwell (whether you stayed at all, not how long). The video_open head is the only weight X has raised from a nonzero value in the published history since August 13. The mechanism appears to be a shift from completion-based signals to attention-holding signals: you now get paid for the open and for keeping someone on the post, but not for them reaching a quality-view threshold. This contradicts the common advice to optimize for finish rate on X video.
move: For X video, optimize the first three seconds to prevent an immediate swipe-away rather than building to a payoff that rewards completion. The dwell head now pays what the finish bonus used to pay.

headline: Off-platform links in X posts showed 33% fewer median likes in 21,864-post sample
statContext: 2,626 posts with genuine off-platform links versus posts without them, from 7,829 accounts over 236 days, relevance-ranked sample
why: The headline number appears in a researcher-audited observational study that corrected for a methodological error: searching post text for 'http' showed a positive association, but filtering for genuine off-platform destination hosts showed negative. The study itself does not claim this proves an algorithmic penalty—linked posts may differ in intent, topic, format, author, and audience. X's For You feed uses many personalized signals, not a single public link multiplier. The mechanism is likely selection bias: people write different kinds of posts when they include links, and those posts attra
move: Test links in your own account rather than treating this as a universal rule. The same study found linked posts got fewer views but more bookmarks, which suggests they serve a reference function rather than a reach function.

headline: Replies and retweets outweigh likes roughly 2-to-1 in X's open-source ranking weights
statContext: Weights from X's 2023 open-sourced ranking code, widely cited across third-party analyses
why: X open-sourced its For You ranking code in 2023 and the relative weights have been public since then, so this is not new. The mechanism is that X's algorithm treats engagement types as predictions of future engagement: a retweet exposes the post to a new network, so it signals broader appeal. A like is private feedback. The code also shows negative actions (blocks, reports, mutes) carry weights several times larger than positive ones in the opposite direction, which means suppression is faster than amplification.
move: Optimize posts for replies and retweets, not just likes. Ask a question, make a claim people want to argue with, or write something people want to add to. A single retweet is worth roughly two likes in the ranking system.

headline: LinkedIn posts with 61+ seconds dwell hit 15.6% engagement versus 1.2% for 0-3 seconds
stat: 15.6% engagement rate at 61+ seconds dwell versus 1.2% at 0-3 seconds
statContext: AuthoredUp dataset, sample size not disclosed, LinkedIn officially documents dwell time as a top signal
why: LinkedIn officially names dwell time as the one feed signal it documents in depth, and this third-party dataset quantifies the relationship. The mechanism is that LinkedIn's three-stage ranking flow (spam filter, small-sample engagement test, network-relevance ranking) uses dwell as a proxy for content quality: if someone stops scrolling to read, the system infers the post is worth showing to more people in that person's network. Thoughtful comments amplify this further. The pattern was already widely known among LinkedIn creators.
move: Write posts that earn long dwell time: open with a hook that makes someone stop scrolling, then deliver enough substance that they stay for a minute. Use line breaks and short paragraphs so the post looks readable at a glance.
